text: A Connection is just a stored record — a conn_id and some fields. Something still has to turn that record into a real, live connection your code can use. That something is a Hook: a Python class that looks up a Connection, reads its fields, and hands you back a working connection.

Here's SnowflakeHook in action: hook equals SnowflakeHook with the conn_id, then hook.get_pandas_df runs real SQL against real Snowflake — the exact same query you'd type in the Snowflake worksheet. The Hook did the work of turning that conn_id into an authenticated session.

A Hook is the low-level interface — give me a working connection, let me run arbitrary commands. An Operator is a higher-level, task-shaped wrapper with retries and logging already handled. Many Operators are thin wrappers around a Hook.

Roughly what SnowflakeOperator does internally: it builds a SnowflakeHook from the conn_id, then calls hook.run with the SQL. The Operator exists so you don't have to write that Hook-calling code yourself for the common case.

Use an existing Operator whenever one already does the job — that's most of the time. Reach for a Hook directly when the logic is more than "run this SQL": branching on a result, pulling data into pandas, calling several methods in sequence.
Next lesson: Provider packages — where connection types like "Snowflake" and their matching Hooks and Operators actually come from.
